lessons.title: The Social Construction of Crime and Deviance

before.exam_tip_html: The command word “Define” asks you to provide a clear sociological meaning for a term — not an example of it. Students often write “deviance is when someone does something that breaks the rules, like stealing” and lose a mark because “like stealing” replaces the definition with an example. A strong definition of deviance would read: “behaviour that violates the social norms of a group or society.” Each mark on a 2-mark Define question typically corresponds to one element of the definition — so adding a qualifying clause (“whether or not it is illegal”) earns the second mark. On the 12-mark Discuss, examiners reward students who present the views of at least two named sociologists or perspectives and reach a supported conclusion. One-sided answers that only present the interactionist view, for example, cannot reach the Mastering tier.
before.content_html:
Crime and Deviance: Two Distinct Concepts

One of the first distinctions sociology asks you to make is between crime and deviance. These concepts overlap but are not the same thing. A crime is an act that breaks the formal law; deviance is any behaviour that violates the unwritten social norms of a group or society. Many deviant acts are not criminal — queue-jumping, belching loudly in a restaurant or wearing a swimsuit to a funeral all break social expectations but carry no legal penalty. Equally, some criminal acts are not widely regarded as deviant — many motorists who exceed the speed limit by a small amount do not consider themselves “criminals” in any meaningful social sense.

This distinction matters because sociology treats both crime and deviance as social constructs — they are not fixed, objective categories but are defined and redefined by societies, institutions and individuals over time.

Key Fact

Crime and deviance are related but distinct: crime breaks the formal law; deviance violates social norms. Some acts are only one of these; only some are both. Sociology studies both as social constructs that change across time, place and situation.

Formal and Informal Rules

Societies regulate behaviour through two types of rules. Formal rules are codified in law and backed by state sanctions: fines, imprisonment or community service. Informal rules — sometimes called social norms — govern everyday behaviour through informal pressure: social disapproval, ridicule or exclusion from the group. A student who arrives late to every lesson is breaking an informal norm; a student who commits fraud is breaking a formal rule. Both are forms of deviance in the sociological sense, but only the second is a crime.

Societies use sanctions to enforce both types of rules. Positive sanctions reward conformity (a round of applause, a pay rise, social praise); negative sanctions punish deviation (a fine, a prison sentence, social exclusion). The relationship between formal law and informal norms is itself a sociological question: laws tend to reflect the norms of the dominant groups in society, a point Marxist and feminist perspectives challenge.

The Relativity of Deviance

A key insight of sociology is that deviance is relative: what counts as deviant varies across time, place and social situation. Three dimensions of relativity are particularly important.

Across time: Acts that were once legal can become criminal — fox hunting with dogs was a lawful rural tradition in England and Wales until the Hunting Act 2004 made it a criminal offence. Conversely, acts once treated as crimes can be decriminalised or legalised — homosexual acts between consenting adult men were criminal offences in England and Wales until the Sexual Offences Act 1967 partially decriminalised them. The law changes as the values and power structures of society change.

Across place: The same act may be legal in one country but criminal in another. Cannabis possession is legal for recreational use in the Netherlands under certain conditions but remains a criminal offence in England and Wales. Drinking alcohol in a public place is unremarkable in most of the United Kingdom but constitutes a serious offence in countries that enforce strict religious law. These cross-cultural variations demonstrate that crime is not an inherent property of an act but a label applied by a society.

Across situation: Context shapes whether an act is considered deviant. Killing another person is treated as murder in most contexts but may be regarded as heroic in warfare, or legally permitted as self-defence. A surgeon cutting open a patient's body with a scalpel is performing a legitimate medical procedure; the same action outside that context would be an assault. Interactionist sociologists like Becker emphasised that deviance is not a quality of the act itself but is created by the reactions of audiences to the act.

Sociological Perspectives on the Social Construction of Crime

Different sociological perspectives explain the social construction of crime in contrasting ways, reflecting deeper disagreements about the nature of society.

A very common examination error is to treat crime and deviance as synonyms. They are overlapping but distinct categories. The simplest way to keep them separate is to think of two overlapping circles: the left circle is all criminal acts, the right circle is all deviant acts. The overlap in the middle is acts that are both criminal and widely seen as deviant (such as violent assault). The left-only region is acts that are criminal but not seen as deviant by most people (minor speeding). The right-only region is acts that are deviant but not criminal (being rude to a stranger). On an exam question asking you to “define deviance”, giving a legal definition will lose marks.

Functionalist perspective: From a functionalist viewpoint, crime and deviance are defined relative to the value consensus of society. Durkheim argued that some level of crime is normal and even functional in any society — it helps clarify the boundaries of acceptable behaviour and, when punished, reaffirms shared values. On this view, defining something as “criminal” is the community expressing its moral boundaries.

Marxist perspective: Marxist sociologists argue that criminal law is not a neutral reflection of shared values but an instrument of class power. The bourgeoisie shape the law to protect their property and interests, criminalising acts common among the working class (street theft) while failing to criminalise or leniently treating harmful acts by the powerful (corporate fraud, tax evasion). The social construction of “crime” therefore reflects and reinforces class inequality.

Feminist perspective: Feminist sociologists point out that laws have historically been made predominantly by men and have often reflected patriarchal interests. Many acts of violence against women — marital rape, for instance — were not defined as criminal in England and Wales until relatively recently (rape within marriage was only conclusively criminalised in R v R, 1991). Definitions of crime and deviance therefore embed gender power relations, and feminist research examines how the social construction of crime affects women both as victims and as offenders.

Interactionist perspective: Interactionists such as Becker argue that no act is inherently criminal or deviant; it becomes so only when a label is successfully applied to it by someone with the power to make the label stick. The social construction of crime is an ongoing process of labelling, negotiation and reaction. Becker used the term moral entrepreneurs to describe individuals and groups who actively campaign for certain behaviours to be defined as deviant or criminal — pressure groups lobbying for new legislation are a contemporary example.

Key Fact

Four perspectives explain social construction differently: functionalists see crime as defined by shared values; Marxists see law as serving the ruling class; feminists see law as historically shaped by patriarchal power; interactionists focus on labelling as the mechanism by which acts become “criminal” or “deviant”.

Law and Morality: Are They the Same?

A final dimension of the social construction of crime is the relationship between law and morality. Not everything that is morally condemned is illegal, and not everything that is illegal is morally condemned by all members of society. Lying to a friend is widely regarded as morally wrong but carries no legal penalty. Some individuals regard civil disobedience — breaking an unjust law — as a moral act. The gap between law and morality varies across time and culture and is itself a product of social processes. Sociologists are interested in who gets to define the law, whose morality it encodes, and whose behaviour it criminalises — questions that run through the entire sociology of crime and deviance.

before.content_html:
Why Do Rates of Crime Vary Across Social Groups?

Sociology asks not just what crime is, but who commits it, and why certain social groups appear in crime statistics more than others. Official figures and self-report studies consistently show that rates of offending are not evenly spread across society. They vary by social class, gender, ethnicity and age. Sociological perspectives disagree sharply about what drives these patterns and what they actually mean.

Key Fact

The four main factors sociologists identify as affecting criminal behaviour are social class, gender, ethnicity and age. Each factor is interpreted differently by functionalist, Marxist, feminist and interactionist perspectives.

Social Class and Crime

Police-recorded crime and self-report studies both suggest that working-class individuals are overrepresented in offending data, particularly for street crime, theft and burglary. However, sociological perspectives explain this in very different ways.

From a functionalist standpoint, Robert Merton’s strain theory argues that crime results from a mismatch between the shared cultural goal of material success and the unequal availability of legitimate means to achieve it. Those with fewer educational qualifications and employment prospects are more likely to turn to “innovation” — using illegal means to achieve socially approved goals. This places working-class individuals at higher risk, but Merton does not treat their criminality as inevitable or biologically determined.

Albert Cohen, writing in Delinquent Boys (1955), developed a subculture theory that extends Merton’s account. Cohen argued that working-class boys share the same success goals as the rest of society, but that educational failure and poor employment prospects leave them unable to achieve those goals through legitimate routes. The resulting status frustration leads them to reject mainstream values and create an alternative status hierarchy within a delinquent subculture. Within that subculture, status is gained through activities such as theft, vandalism and truancy rather than through school or work. A successful thief earns prestige from peers in a way that the school system denies him.

Critics of Cohen point out that not all working-class young people form delinquent subcultures, and that his theory assumes working-class youths internalise mainstream goals in the first place. Some sociologists argue instead that working-class young men may actively reject those goals rather than feel frustrated by failing to achieve them.

Marxist perspectives challenge the focus on working-class crime altogether. They argue that the law is shaped in the interests of the bourgeoisie, meaning that white-collar crime (fraud, tax evasion, corporate harm) committed by more powerful groups attracts less police attention and lighter sentencing. The official statistics therefore exaggerate working-class criminality not because working-class people commit more harm, but because their crimes are more visible and more likely to be prosecuted.

A common error is to treat crime statistics as proving that working-class people are naturally more criminal. Sociologists reject this. Official crime figures record crimes that are reported and prosecuted. Marxists argue that white-collar and corporate crimes cause enormous financial and physical harm (unsafe working conditions, fraudulent financial products) but receive far less police attention. The overrepresentation of working-class individuals in the statistics may reflect policing priorities and legal definitions as much as actual behaviour. Always distinguish the pattern in the data from the explanation for that pattern.

Gender and Crime

Men commit the large majority of recorded crimes in England and Wales. Official figures consistently show that male offenders account for roughly three-quarters of all prosecutions. Sociologists offer several explanations for this gender gap.

Functionalist accounts emphasise gender socialisation: boys are socialised to be tough, assertive and risk-taking, traits that make criminality more likely. Girls are socialised towards conformity, care and domestic roles, making deviance less likely. This explanation treats gender roles as functional for social order.

Frances Heidensohn, writing in Women and Crime (1985) from a feminist perspective, offers a more structural account using control theory. Heidensohn argues that women commit fewer crimes because patriarchal society controls them far more effectively than it controls men. In the home, women are expected to spend their time on housework and childcare; those who challenge these expectations risk male violence as an assertion of patriarchal authority. In public, women are controlled by the threat of sexual violence and the fear that “inappropriate” behaviour will damage their reputation. At work, women face male-dominated hierarchies and sexual harassment. This web of patriarchal control restricts women’s opportunities for deviance far more than equivalent controls restrict men.

Pat Carlen, in Women, Crime and Poverty (1988), studied 39 working-class women who had been convicted of criminal offences, using in-depth unstructured interviews. Carlen also draws on control theory but foregrounds class alongside gender. She argues that women are controlled through two kinds of deal. The class deal promises working-class women consumer goods and a respectable lifestyle in exchange for their labour. The gender deal offers psychological and material rewards through a male breadwinner in exchange for love and domestic labour. When either or both deals break down — through unemployment, poverty or abusive relationships — crime becomes a rational choice because the usual incentives for conformity are absent. Carlen’s work has been critiqued for its small sample size, but it is important because it connects women’s criminality to structural inequality rather than individual pathology.

Ethnicity and Crime

Official statistics show that Black individuals are overrepresented in stop-and-search figures and in prison populations relative to their share of the general population. Sociologists treat this as a pattern requiring critical analysis, not as evidence of inherently higher criminality.

Key Fact

Overrepresentation of ethnic minorities in crime statistics is explained by sociologists through: (1) interactionist labelling and selective policing; (2) Marxist arguments about institutional racism; and (3) structural explanations linking poverty and deprivation to crime rates. No perspective treats the pattern as proof of biological difference.

From an interactionist standpoint, the overrepresentation reflects policing practices rather than offending behaviour. Becker’s labelling theory suggests that the police apply stereotyped labels to young Black men, making them more likely to be stopped and searched, arrested and charged. The label “criminal” then becomes a master status that shapes how the individual is treated by courts and employers, increasing the risk of further offending through a self-fulfilling prophecy.

A Marxist perspective connects racial inequality in the criminal justice system to wider structural inequalities. Ethnic minorities are disproportionately represented among those in poverty and those in low-paid, insecure employment. If crime is partly driven by material deprivation, then economic marginalisation explains some of the overrepresentation. Additionally, Marxists point to institutional racism in policing and the courts as reproducing racial inequality through the criminal justice system itself.

Examining patterns in crime data by ethnicity is a legitimate and important sociological task, but it requires critical awareness. The Macpherson Report (1999) into the Metropolitan Police’s handling of Stephen Lawrence’s murder concluded that the force was “institutionally racist”, giving a UK context to the interactionist and Marxist arguments above. Sociologists consistently emphasise that the data shows overrepresentation in police-recorded outcomes — which reflect policing choices — and that stop-and-search rates cannot be used as straightforward evidence of higher offending. Any analysis should name the mechanisms being proposed (selective policing, institutional racism, material deprivation) rather than leaving the pattern unexplained.

Age and Crime

Crime data consistently shows that offending peaks in late adolescence and early adulthood, with the highest rates among those aged 15 to 24. Sociological explanations draw on both structural and interactionist factors. From a functionalist perspective, young people may have less stake in conformity — they are less likely to own property, hold stable employment or have family responsibilities that make law-abiding behaviour rewarding. Cohen’s delinquent subculture theory is particularly relevant here, as it focuses specifically on young working-class men. From an interactionist standpoint, young people are more likely to be subject to police surveillance and labelling, which inflates their recorded crime rates beyond their actual offending.

Crime as a Public Issue

Crime is not just a legal matter — it is also a subject of intense public and political debate. How much crime is there? How should offenders be punished? Are young offenders treated too leniently? Does prison work? And how much of what people believe about crime comes from lived experience rather than from the media? These questions divide sociologists, politicians and the public, and different sociological perspectives offer sharply different answers.

Key Fact

The AQA specification identifies five areas of public debate over crime: concerns over violent crime, sentencing, the treatment of young offenders, the prison system, and media coverage of crime. Each is contested between sociological perspectives.

Concerns Over Violent Crime

Public concern about violent crime has been a persistent feature of UK public debate. Knife crime in particular attracted sustained political and media attention during the 2000s and 2010s, with campaigns, policy initiatives and moral panics surrounding youth violence in cities including London, Manchester and Birmingham.

Sociologists note an important distinction between the fear of crime and actual crime rates. The Crime Survey for England and Wales consistently shows that many people, especially older adults and women, report high levels of fear of crime in contexts where their statistical likelihood of victimisation is relatively low. This fear-reality gap suggests that public perception of violent crime is shaped by factors beyond direct experience — including media coverage.

From a functionalist standpoint, concern about violent crime serves an integrative function: the collective response to crime — including public outrage, law enforcement and sentencing — reinforces shared values and social solidarity. Crime, from this perspective, is a normal feature of social life whose control reaffirms the moral boundaries of society.

Marxist perspectives are more critical of the focus on violent street crime. They argue that the framing of crime debates in terms of working-class street violence diverts public attention from corporate and state harm, which may cause more damage in aggregate. For example, unsafe working environments, environmental pollution and financial misconduct may injure or cost far more lives than street violence, yet attract less sustained political attention.

Sentencing, Young Offenders and the Prison System

Debates about sentencing centre on whether punishment should emphasise retribution (making offenders pay for their crimes), deterrence (discouraging future offending), rehabilitation (reforming offenders so they do not re-offend) or incapacitation (removing offenders from society). Different sociological and political perspectives weigh these goals very differently.

New Right perspectives tend to favour tougher sentencing and longer prison terms as deterrents, arguing that lenient sentencing encourages a dependency culture in which offenders face insufficient consequences. They are sceptical about rehabilitation programmes and more sympathetic to punitive approaches. Marxist perspectives counter that prison populations are disproportionately drawn from the poorest social groups, and that imprisonment addresses the symptoms of inequality rather than its causes. Imprisoning working-class individuals does not resolve poverty, unemployment or social marginalisation, and high reoffending rates suggest that incarceration alone is ineffective at reducing crime.

The treatment of young offenders is a particularly contested area. In England and Wales, the age of criminal responsibility is ten — among the lowest in Europe. Interactionist perspectives warn that criminalising young people early attaches a deviant label that becomes a master status, reducing their employment prospects, social relationships and self-image in ways that make further offending more likely. Feminist perspectives add that young women in contact with the youth justice system are often treated as having failed not just the law but also gender norms, facing additional stigma around their sexual behaviour and family roles.

Functionalist view: prison and sentencing reinforce shared social norms by marking the boundaries between acceptable and unacceptable behaviour. The goal is social solidarity, not just individual deterrence.

Marxist view: prison serves the interests of the ruling class by removing and controlling the most marginalised members of the working class. High reoffending rates reveal that prison does not address the structural causes of crime.

Interactionist view: labelling theory predicts that imprisonment reinforces criminal identities. Once a person is publicly labelled a criminal, opportunities for legitimate employment and social reintegration narrow, making further offending more likely.

Feminist view: women in prison are often victims of domestic abuse, poverty and mental health difficulties. A punishment-focused system fails to address these structural inequalities, and incarceration may further damage women’s wellbeing without reducing the conditions that led to their offending.

The Media and Crime

The media plays a central role in shaping public perceptions of crime. Sociologists have identified several ways in which media coverage systematically distorts the picture of crime that most people receive.

News values shape which crimes are reported. Newsworthy crimes tend to be dramatic, violent, unusual or involving well-known individuals. This means that murder, serious assault and sexual crimes receive disproportionate coverage relative to their actual frequency, while more common crimes such as property theft receive far less. The result is that media audiences overestimate both the prevalence and the severity of violent crime.

Selective reporting also shapes the profile of offenders shown in the media. If certain social groups (young working-class men, or members of ethnic minorities) are consistently shown as the perpetrators of crime, the cumulative effect may be to associate those groups with criminality in the public mind, reinforcing stereotypes that then feed back into policing practices.

Key Fact

A moral panic is a period of intense public concern about a perceived social threat, often amplified by the media. The group identified as the source of that threat is labelled a folk devil. Classic UK examples include the 1960s panic about mods and rockers, and the 2000s–2010s panic around knife crime and youth gangs.

Moral Panics and Folk Devils

The concept of the moral panic was developed by sociologist Stanley Cohen (not to be confused with Albert Cohen). In Folk Devils and Moral Panics (1972), Cohen studied the media reaction to clashes between mods and rockers at Clacton in 1964. He found that newspaper coverage dramatically exaggerated the scale of the disorder, transforming a relatively minor incident into a major social threat. The media identified the groups involved as folk devils — the mods and rockers became the symbolic embodiment of social breakdown and moral decline. The disproportionate police and court response that followed Cohen described as a deviancy amplification spiral: media coverage increased public anxiety, led to more aggressive policing, which produced more arrests and more coverage, which amplified anxiety further.

More recent UK examples illustrate the continued relevance of the concept. Concerns about knife crime among young people in urban areas from the mid-2000s onwards generated intense media coverage, political debate and policing initiatives. Sociologists have debated how far this coverage reflected a genuine rise in knife violence and how far it amplified and distorted the picture, with some arguing that the panic led to disproportionate stop-and-search activity targeting young Black men in particular.

From a Marxist perspective, moral panics serve an ideological function: by directing public concern towards the crimes of marginalised groups, they distract attention from the crimes of powerful elites. From an interactionist perspective, moral panics illustrate how the meaning of crime is socially constructed through the interaction of media, police, courts and public. From a feminist perspective, moral panics about violent youth often reinforce racialised and gendered stereotypes, with particular consequences for how young Black men and young women are policed.

A frequent misconception is that the media simply reports crime as it is, making media coverage a reliable indicator of crime trends. Sociologists reject this. News values prioritise dramatic, violent and unusual incidents, meaning violent crime is systematically overreported relative to property crime. Moral panic theory shows that media coverage can construct a sense of crisis that goes far beyond the statistical reality. Always distinguish between official crime statistics, victim survey data and media representations when assessing claims about crime trends.
